opus-5.5.text:
I think high-school projects are valuable, though usually not in the way people expect. When you're building your first résumé, nobody is really evaluating whether your project was technically impressive. A recruiter or a professor knows a seventeen-year-old's app isn't going to be production-grade. What they're looking for is signal: did you build something because you were curious, did you finish it, and can you talk about it honestly?

The finishing part matters a lot. Plenty of people start things. Far fewer get a project to the point where someone else can actually use it, even if that's just a few classmates or a small online community. That last stretch, where you fix the boring bugs, write the documentation, and deal with users who don't behave the way you imagined, is where you learn the most. It's also what makes the project worth putting on a résumé.

Then there's what happens in the conversation. A résumé line gets you into the room, but the project really pays off when someone asks, "Why did you build it this way?" and you can explain your trade-offs, your mistakes, and what you'd do differently. That shows how you think, and how you think is what people are actually hiring for early on.

I'd also caution people against treating projects as résumé decoration. If you pick something only because it sounds impressive, like an "AI-powered platform" you lost interest in after two weeks, it tends to come through when you talk about it. A smaller project you genuinely cared about, maybe a tool that solved an annoying problem at your school, is usually more compelling because the motivation is real and the details are vivid.

So my view is that the project itself matters less than what it shows: that you can take an idea from nothing to something real, and that you learned from doing it. That's a habit that compounds, and starting it in high school gives you a real head start.

r002.rationale: It describes a project as a résumé signal that an applicant follows through, makes something others can use, and discusses it honestly—evidence of traits others can trust.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think most people get this backwards. They treat high-school projects as line items, things to list so the résumé isn't empty. But a hiring manager or an admissions reader isn't counting entries. They're looking for evidence that you can take something from nothing to done, and that you actually cared about it.

So the value of a high-school project isn't the project itself. It's the story it lets you tell. If you built a weather station from an Arduino and some sensors, nobody cares that it reported the temperature. They care that the first version drifted two degrees and you figured out it was heat from the board itself, and you moved the sensor. That's the whole thing. That one detail tells someone you debug, you don't give up, and you understand your own system.

My advice is to be ruthless about it. Pick one or two projects you can talk about for twenty minutes without notes. Drop the rest, even if dropping them makes the page look thinner. A thin résumé with one real story beats a full page of things you half-remember. And write them in terms of what went wrong and what you did about it, not what the project was supposed to do.

The other thing I'd say, and this surprised me when I started interviewing people, is that unfinished projects are fine if you're honest about why. "I abandoned this because I realized the approach couldn't scale" is a mature thing to say at seventeen. Pretending it was finished, and getting caught in the follow-up question, is not.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re valuable because, when you’re building your first résumé, you may not have much formal work experience yet. A technical project gives you something concrete to talk about: what you wanted to build, what you actually did, and how you worked through problems.

It doesn’t have to be a huge or groundbreaking project. A small project you understand well can say a lot about your initiative and ability to learn. On the résumé, I’d focus on your contribution and the result, rather than just listing the technologies you used. And if it was a team project, be clear about which part was yours.

A small project that you understand well—and can explain honestly—can show curiosity, initiative, and an ability to learn. I’d focus less on listing technologies and more on what you actually did and what you learned.
